study_identification_part.si4_title: Multiscale heterogeneity of functional connectivity in autism

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Support vector regression (SVR) with 5-fold cross-validation was used to predict clinical and cognitive measures from FC deviation scores at connection, region, and network levels. Variables included: ADOS social affect, ADOS RRB, ADI RRB, ADI communication, ADI social interaction, Social Responsiveness Scale-2 (SRS), full-scale IQ (WASI-II), Short Sensory Profile (SSP), and Autism Quotient (AQ). PCA was applied to reduce dimensionality (50% variance explained). Linear SVR with epsilon-insensitive loss was used. Grid-search cross-validation optimized hyperparameters. Predictions were validated on held-out data across 1,000 permutations. Significance assessed via permutation testing with FDR correction. Strength of association quantified by correlation between predicted and observed scores (median across 5 folds reported). Group differences in deviation overlap were assessed using permutation tests (10,000 permutations) with FDR correction at connection, region, and network levels. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests compared total extreme deviation counts between groups. Independent t-tests compared ratios of positive-to-negative deviations. Sensitivity analyses controlled for sex, ADHD comorbidity, and medication use.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Autism showed extreme heterogeneity at the connection level (no more than 3.4% overlap), but higher convergence at region and network levels, with greater overlap of negative deviations in sensory-motor areas and positive deviations in transmodal systems (default mode and frontoparietal networks).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Connection-level heterogeneity was very high, with no single connection deviating in more than 3.4% of individuals in either group. No significant group differences in total extreme deviation counts or positive-to-negative deviation ratios were found. At the regional level, autistic individuals showed significantly greater overlap for negative (reduced FC) deviations in sensory-motor, anterior insula, prefrontal, temporal pole, visual, and medial temporal regions, and greater overlap for positive (increased FC) deviations in medial prefrontal, superior frontal, cingulate, inferior parietal lobules, and subcortical areas. At the network level, autism showed greater overlap for negative deviations within visual, ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and for connections linking somatomotor network to visual, dorsal attention, and ventral attention networks. Greater overlap for positive deviations was found in default mode network and frontoparietal network connections, and in subcortical-cortical connections. FC deviations significantly predicted full-scale IQ and SRS at connection level (r=0.16 and 0.29, p<0.001); IQ and SRS at regional level (r=0.1, p<0.02); and ADI social, AQ, and SRS at network level (r=0.17-0.18, p<0.02). Findings were robust to sex, ADHD comorbidity, and medication effects.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study demonstrates that multiscale analysis is essential for understanding autism heterogeneity. Extreme connection-level heterogeneity may explain inconsistent findings in the FC literature and represents a neural substrate for individual clinical differences. Higher regional and network-level convergence suggests shared neural phenotypes characterized by reduced FC in somatomotor systems and increased FC in transmodal association networks, potentially reflecting imbalanced sensorimotorassociation axis signaling. Different scales of FC organization relate to distinct clinical features: connection and regional levels predict IQ and broad social responsiveness (SRS), while network-level organization predicts more specific social functioning (ADI social) and broader autistic traits (AQ). The approach exemplifies moving beyond group mean comparisons to characterize individual variability.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The analysis relies on threshold choices for defining extreme deviations and computing overlap, though robustness across thresholds was demonstrated. Cerebellum was excluded due to poor scan coverage in many participants, despite its known role in autism pathophysiology. The sample had imbalanced sex ratios between autism and control groups (reflecting natural prevalence), with underrepresentation of autistic females. Supplementary materials referenced for key details (QC procedures, preprocessing, model validation) are not available in the main text. The study cannot determine whether the identified neural phenotype represents a subgroup of autism or a broader characteristic.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a preprint posted on medRxiv (not peer-reviewed). The study applies normative modeling to functional connectivity data at multiple spatial scales, which is a novel approach compared to previous normative modeling studies in autism that focused on structural measures (e.g., cortical thickness, grey matter volume). Data came from 32 different scanning sites across three multi-site datasets. ComBat harmonization was applied to site effects before normative modeling rather than modeling site effects within the normative framework. The study used 390 ROIs after excluding 24 regions with poor coverage. Functional connectivity was calculated using Pearson correlation and normalized using Gaussian-gamma mixture modeling. The normative models were trained only on neurotypical individuals and applied to autism individuals for deviation quantification. Cross-validation (10-fold) was used only for the NT group. Clinical measures came from multiple instruments: ADOS-2, ADI-R, SRS-2, WASI-II, SSP, and AQ. Not all clinical measures were available for all participants (see Table 1 for sample sizes per measure). The study included sensitivity analyses for sex, ADHD comorbidity, and medication use (Supplement Section 10, Table S4). Authors note this work aligns with and extends previous findings by Segal et al., 2022 on grey matter volume heterogeneity in autism.
